module_title: Feed Formulation for Health and Disease Challenges

lessons.title: Nutritional Strategies to Support Gut Health
lessons.body:
A healthy gut is the first line of defence against disease. In pigs, the gut must digest feed, absorb nutrients, and keep harmful bacteria like E. coli and Salmonella from taking over. You can support gut health through feed formulation without buying expensive medicines. First, include highly digestible ingredients. For example, use cooked or extruded soybeans instead of raw full-fat soybeans; raw soybeans contain trypsin inhibitors that irritate the gut. Also, fine grinding helpsâgrind maize and other grains to a particle size of 600â800 microns. Too coarse, and nutrients are locked away; too fine, and you risk ulcers.

Second, add fibre carefully. Moderate levels of fermentable fibre, such as 5â10% sugar beet pulp or 3â5% soy hulls, feed beneficial bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate. Butyrate is the main energy source for gut cells and reduces inflammation. However, too much fibre (above 15%) can cause diarrhoea in young pigs. In Africa, you can use local by-products: cassava peel meal (dried and detoxified), brewersâ spent grain, or mango seed kernelsâbut always test for toxins and limit inclusion to 10â20% for growers.

Third, manage protein sources. Excess protein ferments in the hindgut, producing ammonia and amines that damage gut lining. Balance amino acids using synthetic lysine, methionine, threonine, and tryptophan so you can lower crude protein by 2â3 percentage points. For a 30â60 kg pig, aim for 16â17% crude protein instead of 18â19%. This simple change reduces diarrhoea and ammonia smell.

Fourth, use organic acids and probiotics. Adding 0.3â0.5% citric acid or 0.2â0.4% formic acid to feed lowers stomach pH, killing pathogens. Probiotics like Lactobacillus or Bacillus subtilis (1Ã10^9 CFU/kg feed) compete with bad bacteria. In Africa, you can ferment feed with local lactic acid bacteriaâmix 1 kg of maize meal with 2 litres of water and 50 ml of yoghurt, let it ferment for 2 days, then mix into 100 kg feed. This is a low-cost way to boost gut health. Always provide clean water, as water quality affects gut directly.

lessons.title: Dietary Approaches to Reduce Post-Weaning Diarrhea
lessons.body:
Post-weaning diarrhea (PWD) is the biggest killer of piglets in Africa, often causing 20â30% mortality. It happens because piglets lose maternal antibodies, their gut is immature, and they face new bacteria and feed. You can reduce PWD through smart formulation. First, wean at 28â35 days, not earlier. At weaning, feed a complex, highly digestible starter diet for 7â10 days. Use cooked cereals: extruded maize, cooked rice, or cooked millet. Avoid raw soybeans; use fermented soy or soy protein concentrate. Include 10â15% skim milk powder or whey powder if affordable; if not, use 5% fish meal and 5% plasma protein (spray-dried porcine plasma) for the first weekâthis is expensive but saves lives.

Second, lower protein. A weaner diet should have 18â20% crude protein, but you can reduce to 16â17% by adding synthetic amino acids. High protein (above 20%) increases undigested protein in the hindgut, feeding E. coli. Also, use zinc oxide at 2,500â3,000 ppm for 14 days post-weaningâthis is a proven tool, but many countries restrict it, so check local rules. In Africa, you can use 1â2% clay (kaolin) or 0.5% charcoal to bind toxins and reduce diarrhea.

Third, add organic acids. Citric acid at 0.5â1% or formic acid at 0.3â0.5% lowers gut pH and inhibits E. coli. You can also use 0.1% essential oils like oregano or thyme. Fourth, manage feed intake. Do not feed piglets ad libitum for the first 3 days; feed small amounts 6â8 times daily. Use a flat tray or mat, not a hopper, to encourage eating. Add 5% glucose or 2% sucrose to the first feed to boost energy. In Africa, many farmers use fermented maize porridge: soak maize in water for 3 days, then mix with starter feed at 1:1. This provides lactic acid and beneficial bacteria. Always provide clean water with electrolytes (1 teaspoon salt + 1 teaspoon sugar per litre) during diarrhea outbreaks.

lessons.title: Feeding for Immune Function and Disease Resistance
lessons.body:
A pigâs immune system needs specific nutrients to fight disease. If you feed for immunity, you reduce antibiotic use and improve survival. First, focus on vitamin A, D, E, and C. Vitamin E at 100â200 IU/kg feed and selenium at 0.3 ppm boost antibody production. In Africa, where grain is often stored long, vitamin E degrades; add a stabilised form or use 5% fresh green forage like sweet potato leaves or amaranth. Vitamin C at 200â500 mg/kg helps under stress, but pigs make their ownâonly supplement during heat or disease.

Second, trace minerals: zinc, copper, iron, and manganese. Zinc at 100â150 ppm (from zinc sulphate) improves gut lining and immune response. Copper at 125â250 ppm (as copper sulphate) has antibacterial effects, but high levels cause toxicity; do not exceed 250 ppm. Iron at 100â150 ppm prevents anaemia. In Africa, use local clay licks or soil if minerals are deficient, but test first.

Third, amino acids. Arginine, glutamine, and threonine are critical for immune cells. Add 0.2% L-glutamine to weaner diets to repair gut. Threonine should be 0.7â0.8% of feed. Also, omega-3 fatty acids from fish oil or flaxseed (2â5%) reduce inflammation. But avoid excess omega-6 from maize oil, which promotes inflammation.

Fourth, use functional feed additives. Beta-glucans from yeast (0.1â0.2%) and mannan-oligosaccharides (MOS) at 0.2â0.5% stimulate immunity. In Africa, you can use 1â2% moringa leaf mealâit contains vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. Also, 0.5% garlic powder or 0.2% turmeric have antimicrobial and immune-boosting effects. Always ensure feed is free of mycotoxins, as they suppress immunity. Store feed dry and use mould inhibitors like 0.2% propionic acid. Finally, provide constant access to clean water; dehydration weakens immunity. During disease outbreaks, increase vitamin E to 300 IU/kg and add 0.3% glutamine for 2 weeks.

lessons.title: Managing Mycotoxin Risks in Pig Diets
lessons.body:
Mycotoxins are poisons made by moulds that grow on feed, especially in warm, humid African conditions. The most dangerous for pigs are aflatoxin, DON (deoxynivalenol), zearalenone, and fumonisin. They cause liver damage, reduced growth, poor immunity, and reproductive failure. You must manage them from field to feed. First, prevent mould growth: harvest grains at low moisture (below 14% for maize), dry quickly on raised platforms or tarpaulins, and store in dry, ventilated bags or silos. Never use mouldy grain, even if you dilute itâtoxins remain.

Second, test your feed. You can use simple ELISA test kits (cost about $5â10 per sample) from agricultural suppliers. If you cannot test, look for signs: musty smell, discoloured grains, or caking. In Africa, aflatoxin is common in groundnuts, maize, and cottonseed. Limit these ingredients: groundnut meal to 5% for growers, 0% for breeders; maize with visible mould to 10% maximum.

Third, use binders. Hydrated sodium calcium aluminosilicate (HSCAS) at 0.5â1% binds aflatoxin. For DON and zearalenone, use yeast cell wall (0.2â0.5%) or activated charcoal (0.5â1%). In Africa, local clay like bentonite (1â2%) can work, but test its binding capacity. Always add binders to the final mix, not to individual ingredients.

Fourth, dilute contaminated feed with clean feed. If aflatoxin is 50 ppb (parts per billion), you can mix 1 part contaminated with 4 parts clean to get 10 ppb, which is safer. But never exceed 20 ppb for young pigs. For zearalenone, keep below 0.5 ppm for gilts. Also, add 0.2% propionic acid or 0.5% vinegar to inhibit mould growth in stored feed. Finally, consider processing: extrusion or roasting at 150Â°C for 30 minutes reduces aflatoxin by 50â80%. In Africa, simple sun-drying on black plastic can reduce moisture and mould. Always store feed in a cool, dry place and use within 4 weeks.

lessons.title: Formulating Diets During Heat Stress
lessons.body:
Heat stress hits pigs hard when temperatures exceed 28Â°C, common in many African regions. Pigs reduce feed intake by 20â50%, so they grow slowly and may die. You can adjust the diet to help. First, increase nutrient density. Because pigs eat less, each bite must pack more energy and protein. Add 2â5% vegetable oil (palm, sunflower, or groundnut oil) to raise energy. Fat also produces less heat during digestion than carbohydrates. For a 50 kg pig, aim for 14 MJ DE/kg instead of 13 MJ. Increase synthetic amino acids (lysine, methionine, threonine) by 10â15% to compensate for lower feed intake.

Second, lower crude protein. High protein increases heat production. Reduce crude protein by 2â3 percentage points and add synthetic amino acids. For example, a grower diet can go from 17% to 14% CP with added lysine (0.2%), methionine (0.05%), threonine (0.1%), and tryptophan (0.02%). This reduces heat load.

Third, adjust fibre. Too much fibre increases heat production. Keep crude fibre below 5% for growers. Avoid high-fibre ingredients like wheat bran or rice bran above 10%. Instead, use cooked or extruded grains.

Fourth, add electrolytes. Heat stress causes loss of potassium and sodium. Add 0.3â0.5% potassium chloride (or 0.5% salt) and 0.2% sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) to feed. Also, add 200â500 mg/kg vitamin C and 100â200 IU/kg vitamin E to reduce oxidative stress. In Africa, you can offer fresh green forage like sweet potato vines or water spinach, which are high in water and electrolytes.

Fifth, manage feeding time. Feed during cooler hoursâearly morning and evening. Wet feeding (mixing feed with 2â3 parts water) increases intake and cools the pig. In Africa, many farmers use fermented wet feed. Always provide unlimited clean water; a lactating sow needs 20â30 litres per day. Add electrolytes to water: 1 teaspoon salt + 1 teaspoon baking soda per 10 litres. Finally, use shade, fans, or sprinklersâdiet alone cannot fix heat stress.

lessons.title: Nutritional Interventions for Respiratory and Enteric Diseases
lessons.body:
Respiratory and enteric diseases are common in African pig farms, especially in crowded, poorly ventilated pens. You can use nutrition to reduce severity and support recovery. For respiratory diseases like pneumonia (caused by Mycoplasma, Pasteurella, or Actinobacillus), focus on antioxidants and anti-inflammatories. Add vitamin E (200â300 IU/kg) and selenium (0.3 ppm) to protect lung tissue. Vitamin C (300â500 mg/kg) reduces inflammation. Omega-3 fatty acids from fish oil (2â3%) or flaxseed (5%) help. Also, add 0.2% L-glutamine and 0.1% L-arginine to support immune cells in lungs. In Africa, moringa leaf meal (2â5%) provides vitamins and anti-inflammatory compounds. Keep dust low by using pelleted or slightly moistened feedâdust irritates lungs.

For enteric diseases like swine dysentery (Brachyspira), salmonellosis, or ileitis (Lawsonia), nutrition is key. First, lower protein: reduce crude protein by 2â3% and add synthetic amino acids. High protein feeds harmful bacteria. Second, add organic acids: 0.5% citric acid or 0.3% formic acid lowers gut pH. Third, use zinc oxide (2,500 ppm for 2 weeks) for diarrhea, but check regulations. Fourth, add 0.2â0.5% mannan-oligosaccharides (MOS) or 0.1% beta-glucans to bind bacteria and boost immunity. In Africa, 1â2% charcoal or 1% clay (kaolin) can bind toxins from bacteria. Also, 0.5% garlic powder or 0.2% oregano oil has antibacterial effects.

During outbreaks, increase vitamin E to 300 IU/kg, add 0.3% glutamine, and provide electrolytes in water (1 teaspoon salt + 1 teaspoon sugar per litre). For respiratory disease, ensure good ventilationâammonia levels below 20 ppm. For enteric disease, clean water is critical; add 0.1% chlorine or 0.5% vinegar to drinking water for 3 days. Always isolate sick pigs and feed them a soft, wet mash with 5% glucose for energy. Remember, nutrition supports but does not replace veterinary treatment. Work with a vet for antibiotics when needed.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Feed Formulation for Health and Disease Challenges in African Pig Production

Pig production in Africa sits at the intersection of opportunity and risk. Demand for pork is rising fast in Nigeria, Kenya, Uganda, South Africa, and Ghana, but producers face disease pressure (African Swine Fever, porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, colibacillosis, salmonellosis), mycotoxin-contaminated feedstuffs (aflatoxin, fumonisin, zearalenone), and heat stress that suppresses intake and immunity. Feed represents 60â75% of total production cost in commercial piggeries, so every formulation decision is a business decision. This practical reference translates nutritional science into actionable formulation rules you can apply on-farm or in a small feed mill.

The central principle: you cannot medicate your way out of a feed problem. Health-supportive formulation reduces mortality, lowers veterinary drug costs, improves feed conversion ratio (FCR), and shortens days to market weight â all of which directly protect margin. Below are the core strategies, with reference tables and a checklist for daily use.

1. Nutritional Strategies to Support Gut Health

The gut is the pig's largest immune organ. A healthy gut means tight junctions, a balanced microbiome, and low inflammation. Formulation levers include:

  • Fibre: Moderate inclusion of fermentable fibre (sugar beet pulp, soy hulls, citrus pulp) feeds beneficial bacteria and produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that nourish colonocytes. In Africa, locally available alternatives include cassava peel meal (properly dried), maize bran, and brewers' spent grain. Keep crude fibre in nursery diets below 5% to avoid reducing intake.
  • Organic acids: Formic, lactic, citric, and fumaric acid lower gastric pH, inhibit E. coli and Salmonella, and improve protein digestion. Typical inclusion: 0.5â1.5% in weaner diets.
  • Probiotics and prebiotics: Lactobacillus, Bacillus, and yeast cell wall products (MOS, beta-glucans) support microbial balance. In humid African climates, choose heat-stable, coated products.
  • Zinc oxide: Historically used at pharmacological levels (2,000â3,000 ppm) to control post-weaning diarrhoea, but the EU banned this in 2022 and many African regulators are tightening. Formulate with lower ZnO (150 ppm nutritional) plus acids and probiotics instead.

2. Dietary Approaches to Reduce Post-Weaning Diarrhoea

Post-weaning diarrhoea (PWD) is the single biggest killer of weaner pigs in tropical and sub-tropical Africa, especially where hygiene is marginal. Nutritional control focuses on reducing undigested protein reaching the hindgut and stabilising the microbiome.

  • Lower crude protein by 1â2 percentage points and supplement with crystalline amino acids (lysine, methionine, threonine, tryptophan) to meet requirements without excess nitrogen.
  • Use highly digestible protein sources: fishmeal, soy protein concentrate, cooked full-fat soy, whey powder. Avoid poorly processed local oilseed meals.
  • Include 10â20% cooked rice, cooked maize, or potato starch â highly digestible energy that reduces fermentation.
  • Add 0.3â0.5% sodium butyrate or coated butyric acid; butyrate is the preferred fuel for enterocytes and reduces inflammation.
  • Restrict feed for the first 5â7 days post-weaning (feed 80â90% of ad libitum) to reduce substrate for pathogens.

3. Feeding for Immune Function and Disease Resistance

Immune response is metabolically expensive. During challenge, pigs divert nutrients from growth to defence. Formulation must anticipate this.

  • Vitamin E and selenium: 50â100 IU/kg vitamin E and 0.3 ppm Se (organic Se preferred) support antioxidant defence and antibody response.
  • Vitamin C: 100â200 mg/kg under heat or disease stress; pigs synthesise it but not enough under challenge.
  • Zinc and copper: 100â150 ppm Zn and 15â25 ppm Cu (as sulphate or chelate) support immune cell function. Avoid excess Cu â it antagonises Zn and is environmentally damaging.
  • Omega-3 fatty acids: 1â2% fish oil or linseed oil modulates inflammation. Inland African producers can use locally pressed linseed or chia where available.
  • Arginine and glutamine: 0.2â0.4% L-arginine and 0.5â1% glutamine support immune cell proliferation during enteric challenge.

4. Managing Mycotoxin Risks in Pig Diets

Africa's warm, humid storage conditions make aflatoxin, fumonisin, and zearalenone chronic threats â especially in maize, groundnuts, and cottonseed. Pigs are among the most sensitive species.

Table 1: Mycotoxin Limits and Pig Sensitivity
Mycotoxin Main Source Pig Tolerance (feed) Clinical Effect Mitigation
Aflatoxin B1 Maize, groundnut cake <20 ppb (piglets <10 ppb) Liver damage, reduced growth, immunosuppression Bentonite/clay binder 0.5â1%; source clean maize
Fumonisin B1 Maize <5 ppm Pulmonary oedema, liver damage Yeast cell wall binder; avoid cracked maize
Zearalenone Maize, wheat <0.25 ppm (gilts <0.1 ppm) Vulvovaginitis, infertility, abortion Clay binders; test breeding stock feed
Deoxynivalenol (DON) Wheat, maize <1 ppm Feed refusal, vomiting, reduced gain Dilution, binder, avoid wet grain
Ochratoxin A Maize, barley <0.1 ppm Kidney damage, reduced performance Proper drying <14% moisture; binder

Sources: FAO (2004) Mycotoxin Regulations in 2003 and Current Developments; EU Commission Regulation 2016/1319; FEFAC guidelines. African national standards vary â verify with your local bureau of standards.

5. Formulating Diets During Heat Stress

Heat stress is a year-round reality across much of sub-Saharan Africa. Pigs reduce feed intake by 15â40% when ambient temperature exceeds 28Â°C, which slows growth and worsens FCR. Formulation must compensate through nutrient density and intake support.

Table 2: Nutrient Adjustments Under Heat Stress (growerâfinisher pigs)
Nutrient Thermoneutral Heat Stress Adjustment Rationale
Crude protein 16â18% Lower to 14â16%; add synthetic AA Reduces heat increment of protein metabolism
Lysine (total) 0.95% Increase to 1.05â1.10% Compensate for lower feed intake
Net energy 2,400 kcal/kg Increase to 2,500â2,600 kcal/kg Concentrate energy in smaller intake
Fat inclusion 2â3% 4â6% Lower heat increment than carbohydrate
Crude fibre 4â5% Reduce to 3â4% Fibre increases heat production
Electrolytes Standard Add 0.3â0.5% KCl, 0.2% NaHCOâ Replace sweat losses, maintain acid-base balance
Vitamin C / E Basal 200 mg/kg / 100 IU/kg Antioxidant support under thermal load

Sources: NRC (2012) Nutrient Requirements of Swine; Renaudeau et al. (2012), Animal 6(5):707â728; FAO (2012) Pig Sector Manual.

6. Nutritional Interventions for Respiratory and Enteric Diseases

Respiratory disease (PRRS, Mycoplasma, Actinobacillus) and enteric disease (E. coli, Salmonella, Lawsonia, rotavirus) are the two dominant clinical complexes in African piggeries. Nutrition cannot replace vaccination and biosecurity, but it can reduce severity and cost.

  • Respiratory: Ensure adequate vitamin A (5,000â10,000 IU/kg), vitamin D (1,000â2,000 IU/kg), and zinc for epithelial integrity. Add 0.2â0.5% arginine during outbreaks. Avoid dusty, finely ground feed â use 600â800 micron particle size.
  • Enteric: Combine organic acids, probiotics, and low-protein formulation. During Lawsonia challenge, add 0.3% sodium butyrate and consider 50â100 ppm tiamulin (with veterinary oversight). For Salmonella, acidified feed plus 0.5% formic acid reduces shedding.
  • Water quality: In many African farms, water is the real disease vector. Chlorinate to 2â3 ppm free chlorine and acidify water to pH 4â5 during enteric outbreaks.
â  SAFETY WARNING â MYCOTOXIN AND DRUG RESIDUE RISK

Never feed visibly mouldy maize, groundnut cake, or cottonseed to pigs â even with a binder. Aflatoxin B1 is a potent liver carcinogen and passes into pork and milk. Do not use medicated feed containing antibiotics without veterinary prescription and respect withdrawal periods (typically 5â14 days) before slaughter. Selling pork with drug residues destroys buyer trust and can trigger regulatory action. Store feed below 14% moisture, on pallets, in a dry, ventilated store. Test suspect batches at a certified laboratory before use.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Test raw materials for moisture (<14%) and mycotoxins before mixing â especially maize and groundnut cake.
  2. Lower crude protein by 1â2 points in weaner and grower diets; balance with synthetic lysine, methionine, threonine, tryptophan.
  3. Include organic acids (0.5â1.5% formic/lactic/citric) in all nursery diets.
  4. Add butyrate (0.3â0.5% coated) during weaning and enteric challenge.
  5. Boost vitamin E, C, zinc, and selenium during heat stress and disease outbreaks.
  6. Use a proven mycotoxin binder (bentonite or yeast cell wall) at 0.5â1% when risk is moderate to high.
  7. Increase nutrient density (energy, lysine) and reduce fibre during heat stress; add electrolytes.
  8. Keep feed particle size 600â800 microns to protect gastric and respiratory health.
  9. Document every batch â date, ingredients, inclusion rates, supplier, and any medication. Traceability protects your business.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Good Practices for the Feed Sector (2019)
  • FAO â Manual on the Application of the HACCP System in Mycotoxin Prevention (2001)
  • NRC â Nutrient Requirements of Swine (2012, free summary)
  • WOAH (OIE) â Terrestrial Animal Health Code (feed safety and antimicrobial use)
  • ILRI â Publications on African Pig Systems and Feed Resources

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Pig Feed Formulation. Always validate inclusion rates against local ingredient analysis and consult a qualified animal nutritionist or veterinarian before making major changes to commercial diets.

quiz.q: What particle size should maize be ground to for optimal gut health in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Grinding to 600â800 microns balances digestibility and gut health, avoiding ulcers from too fine particles.

quiz.q: Which short-chain fatty acid is the main energy source for gut cells?
quiz.explanation: Butyrate is the preferred energy source for colonocytes and reduces inflammation.

quiz.q: What is a safe maximum inclusion level of dried cassava peel meal for grower pigs?
quiz.explanation: Cassava peel meal can be used at 10â20% for growers if properly dried and detoxified.

quiz.q: How much can you lower crude protein in a 30â60 kg pig diet by adding synthetic amino acids?
quiz.explanation: Balancing amino acids allows a reduction of 2â3 percentage points, reducing diarrhoea and ammonia.

quiz.q: Which organic acid is commonly added at 0.3â0.5% to lower stomach pH?
quiz.explanation: Formic acid at 0.3â0.5% is effective in reducing gut pathogens.

quiz.q: What is the recommended minimum weaning age to reduce post-weaning diarrhea?
quiz.explanation: Weaning at 28â35 days allows the gut to mature and reduces stress.

quiz.q: Which protein source is best for weaner pigs to reduce diarrhea?
options: B) Fermented soy or soy protein concentrate
quiz.explanation: Fermented soy or soy protein concentrate is highly digestible and low in anti-nutritional factors.

quiz.q: What is the recommended level of zinc oxide for post-weaning diarrhea?
quiz.explanation: 2,500â3,000 ppm zinc oxide for 14 days is a proven tool, but check local regulations.

quiz.q: Which additive can bind toxins and reduce diarrhea in weaner pigs?
quiz.explanation: Clay like kaolin binds bacterial toxins and reduces diarrhea.

quiz.q: How many times per day should weaner pigs be fed for the first 3 days after weaning?
quiz.explanation: Small, frequent meals (6â8 times) encourage eating and reduce gut overload.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is critical for antibody production and should be at 100â200 IU/kg?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin E at 100â200 IU/kg boosts immune response and antibody production.

quiz.q: What is the maximum safe level of copper in pig feed to avoid toxicity?
quiz.explanation: Copper above 250 ppm can cause toxicity; 125â250 ppm is safe and antibacterial.

quiz.q: Which amino acid is critical for gut repair and should be added at 0.2% for weaners?
quiz.explanation: L-glutamine at 0.2% supports gut cell repair and immune function.

quiz.q: Which local feed additive has immune-boosting and antimicrobial effects?
quiz.explanation: Moringa leaf meal contains vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants that boost immunity.

quiz.q: What is the most dangerous mycotoxin for pigs in Africa, often found in groundnuts?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin is common in groundnuts and maize and causes liver damage.

quiz.q: What moisture level should maize be at for safe storage to prevent mould?
quiz.explanation: Maize should be dried to below 14% moisture to prevent mould growth.

quiz.q: Which binder is effective against aflatoxin at 0.5â1% inclusion?
quiz.explanation: HSCAS at 0.5â1% binds aflatoxin effectively.

quiz.q: What is the maximum safe level of aflatoxin in feed for young pigs?
quiz.explanation: Young pigs should not exceed 20 ppb aflatoxin in feed.

quiz.q: Which processing method reduces aflatoxin by 50â80%?
options: B) Extrusion or roasting at 150Â°C for 30 minutes
quiz.explanation: Extrusion or roasting at 150Â°C for 30 minutes destroys a significant portion of aflatoxin.

quiz.q: During heat stress, how much should you increase synthetic amino acids?
quiz.explanation: Increase amino acids by 10â15% to compensate for lower feed intake.

quiz.q: Which electrolyte is added to feed during heat stress to replace losses?
quiz.explanation: Potassium chloride at 0.3â0.5% replaces potassium lost through sweating.

quiz.q: What is the recommended level of vitamin C in feed during heat stress?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin C at 200â500 mg/kg helps reduce oxidative stress during heat.

quiz.q: Which feeding method increases intake and cools pigs during heat stress?
quiz.explanation: Wet feeding (mixing feed with water) increases intake and provides cooling.

quiz.q: How much water does a lactating sow need per day during heat stress?
quiz.explanation: Lactating sows need 20â30 litres of water daily, more in heat.

quiz.q: Which nutrient helps protect lung tissue during respiratory disease?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin E at 200â300 IU/kg protects lung tissue from oxidative damage.

quiz.q: Which additive binds bacteria and boosts immunity during enteric disease?
quiz.explanation: MOS at 0.2â0.5% binds harmful bacteria and stimulates immunity.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended ammonia level in pig housing?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia should be kept below 20 ppm to reduce respiratory irritation.

quiz.q: During a disease outbreak, what should you add to drinking water for 3 days?
quiz.explanation: Chlorine or vinegar in water helps kill pathogens during outbreaks.

quiz.q: Which local feed additive has antibacterial effects and can be used at 0.5%?
quiz.explanation: Garlic powder at 0.5% has antibacterial and immune-boosting properties.

quiz.q: What is the recommended level of fish oil to reduce inflammation in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Fish oil at 2â3% provides omega-3 fatty acids that reduce inflammation.
